title: Labels and the table
subtitle: Reading Bordeaux and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: Bordeaux labels show the château, the appellation, the vintage and often a classification, like Grand Cru Classé en 1855. Appellations run from broad to precise: Bordeaux, Bordeaux Supérieur, then district appellations like Haut-Médoc, then communes like Pauillac. Mis en bouteille au château means estate-bottled. Many châteaux also make a cheaper second wine.

steps.title: Second wines and value
steps.body: Second wines, like Carruades de Lafite or Pavillon Rouge de Château Margaux, use younger vines or lots not chosen for the main wine. They offer a taste of a great estate at a lower price. Côtes de Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur from good producers are often excellent value.
steps.highlight: Second wines and Côtes for value

steps.prompt: Order these appellations from broadest to most precise.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Left Bank reds suit lamb, especially roast leg of lamb, and steak. Right Bank Merlot suits duck, mushrooms and beef. Dry whites from Pessac-Léognan suit fish in butter sauce. Sauternes suits foie gras, Roquefort and fruit tarts. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young.
steps.highlight: Lamb with Pauillac, foie gras with Sauternes

steps.prompt: What does mis en bouteille au château mean?
steps.explanation: Estate-bottled, a sign the château controlled the whole process.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show château, appellation, vintage and classification
Second wines and the Côtes offer value
Lamb suits Left Bank reds; foie gras suits Sauternes
